title: An ethnographic and technological study of breakbeats in Hardcore, Jungle, and Drum & Bass
publication_date: August 2013 (submitted as a PhD thesis to McGill University; cataloged by McGill University Libraries as 2014)
abstract: During the late 1980s and early 1990s, the United Kingdom’s DJ-oriented electronic music community embraced new technologies and developed innovative techniques to master these technologies, resulting in the development of new genres. Three such genres, Hardcore, Jungle, and Drum & Bass (HJDB), emerged at the critical intersection between computer technology and the consumer market, which allowed computer music to be made through the use of home-based studios. The essential instrument in HJDB was the digital sampler, a device that offered musicians the ability to achieve realistic instrumentation through a “cut-and-paste” method of production. The thread that ties these three genres together was their unique usage of fast-paced sampled drums, derived primarily from breakbeats—samples of short percussion solos typically from 1960s to 1980s Funk and Jazz recordings.\nThis dissertation explores a number of important issues that have not been addressed in prior writing on HJDB, and consists of three main objectives. The first is to provide a written history of the genres from the perspective of those that have made the music. This history catalogues the origins of the United Kingdom’s DJ-oriented electronic music genres, the incorporation of breakbeats into this music that created the Hardcore genre, and developments that then resulted in the creation of the Jungle genre and subsequently the Drum & Bass genre. The second objective is to provide an explanation of the main technologies used in the creation of this music (e.g., the digital sampler) and the techniques developed by musicians to harness this technology. The third objective is to provide methods for the computational analysis of HJDB music, through automated determination of the breakbeats being used, detection of downbeat locations, and an estimation of the degree of rhythmic modification. Each of these objectives has been informed by over twenty interviews with musicians and label owners from throughout the history of HJDB. Computational methods based on HJDB-specific knowledge are shown to significantly outperform generalized music analysis techniques, highlighting the importance of style-specific approaches for computational musicology.
summary:
The dissertation combines an ethnographic history of Hardcore, Jungle, and Drum & Bass with a technical account of sampling practices and computational methods for breakbeat analysis. Its principal methodological contribution is the use of genre-specific knowledge—particularly breakbeat timbre, drum patterns, and downbeat structure—to improve automated breakbeat classification and downbeat detection.

The research was subsequently developed into peer-reviewed computational music research. The downbeat-detection component appeared as “One in the Jungle: Downbeat Detection in Hardcore, Jungle, and Drum and Bass” at ISMIR 2012; the paper reports a style-specific method evaluated on 206 HJDB pieces and is listed with 41 SciVal citations by Birmingham City University. ([pureportal.bcu.ac.uk](https://pureportal.bcu.ac.uk/en/publications/one-in-the-jungle-downbeat-detection-in-hardcore-jungle-and-drum--2/)) A later DAFx 2015 paper, “Computational Strategies for Breakbeat Classification and Resequencing in Hardcore, Jungle and Drum & Bass,” extended the breakbeat-classification work by comparing generalized, SVM-based specialized, and deep-network approaches and by reconstructing breakbeat sequences; the publication is listed with six Scopus citations. ([open-access.bcu.ac.uk](https://www.open-access.bcu.ac.uk/3270/))

The thesis itself is cited in later scholarly work, including a 2023 doctoral thesis and the proceedings of ISMIR 2024. ([open-access.bcu.ac.uk](https://www.open-access.bcu.ac.uk/15174/1/Maciej%20Tomczak%20PhD%20Thesis%20published_Final%20version_Submitted%20Jan%202023_Final%20Award%20Nov%202023%20.pdf)) The available evidence supports an impact primarily within computational musicology, music information retrieval, breakbeat analysis, and audio-production research. I found no reliable evidence of direct commercial-industry deployment of the dissertation’s specific algorithms.
